column3: The paired rebuke in the same judgment scene exposes the silence of the presumed objects of support.
Provision and the tribes' wrongdoing do not clarify the collapse of mutual help.
Noah's question about who could protect him from God identifies the limits of human help before divine judgment.
Its matching rhetorical formula rebukes a failure of proper response to God, though not mutual aid.
It identifies those gathered as wrongdoers, their associates, and their objects of worship, setting the scene for the question.
God's sufficiency as Guide and Helper contrasts with the condemned group's inability to supply help for itself.
It directly portrays the Day when a person has neither power nor a helper.
The ensuing exchange among the condemned shows the group whose expected solidarity has failed.
God's promised help for the messengers supplies a clear contrary model of effective support.
It warns wrongdoers that, apart from God, they have no allies and will not be helped.
Reviving dead land and provision do not add to the failed-mutual-help question.
It places the absence of help between patrons in the setting of the decisive Day.
It directly asks whether the beings worshiped besides God can help their devotees or themselves.
It names the objects worshiped besides God immediately before the mutual-help challenge.
Its rhetorical question calls for aid to the oppressed and a helper from God, a constructive contrast to failed aid.
Noah's message and counsel do not elucidate mutual aid at judgment.
Divine aid granting victory to earlier servants offers a contrary source of effective help.
Divine help to the Prophet shares the help theme but not the focus's failed collective support.
It exposes worshiped beings as unable to control harm or benefit, supporting the impotence behind the rebuke.
Rain and vegetation do not clarify the focus question.
The claim that a united group is invincible provides a direct presumption of collective strength that judgment overturns.
Legitimate resistance after oppression concerns a different sense of seeking victory.
The command to halt and question them directly frames the interrogative judgment scene.
Lot's appeal for divine help against corrupt people contrasts true help sought from God with the condemned group's helplessness.

The repeated formula is a rhetorical parallel, but concerns unjust judgment rather than aid.
The final condemnation explicitly says the people of the Fire have no helpers.
God as the excellent Protector and Helper supplies the true alternative to reliance on failed support.
The oath by what is unseen has no material relation to help.
It immediately describes those questioned as surrendered and unable to resist.
God's aid to believers in battle is a broad contrary instance of effective help.
Its rhetorical rebuke has a similar form but concerns refusal of faith, not mutual aid.
Israel's scripture and favors do not clarify the focus question.
God's promised aid to the wronged contrasts divine support with the inability of wrongdoers to assist one another.
Responsibility for another person's purification is unrelated to failed mutual aid.
It immediately depicts the condemned turning to question one another after their support has failed.
It denies any protector or helper besides God, a direct theological boundary for the focus's helpless group.
The final-day address explicitly tells the condemned that they will not be helped.
The description of a drink in Paradise does not develop the judgment scene.
It exposes allies who will not stand by one another when tested, a worldly parallel to failed solidarity.
The coming irreversible Day leaves no refuge or denial, reinforcing the judgment setting of helplessness.
The demand to revive forefathers does not clarify the loss of mutual support.
It asks who can help after God withdraws help, directly clarifying the limits of all other aid.
The account of the slander concerns blame and punishment, not mutual help.
It continues the immediate dialogue by locating responsibility in the condemned group's refusal of faith.
Those cursed by God are said to have no helper, a concise parallel to the focus's terminal helplessness.
The rejection of idol worship does not itself develop the question of mutual aid.
The distinction between righteous and self-wronging descendants does not clarify the focus scene.
It states that victory comes only from God, contrasting the failure of self-supplied collective help.
The rebuke for arguing without knowledge does not add to the focus reading.
The two gushing springs do not clarify aid or judgment.
God's power to aid the oppressed provides a contrary account of where effective help comes from.
The question naming the Inevitable does not add to the mutual-help theme.
The leaders deny any authority over their followers, immediately explaining the group's mutual recrimination.
God's aid and victory share the root but do not address failed support among the condemned.
On the Day, no soul can avail another and none will be helped, closely paralleling collective helplessness.
The gift of the clarifying Book does not develop the focus question.
God's aid at Badr is a broad contrary example of effective help.
The warning against intimate confidants does not clarify the focus's judgment scene.
Guidance on grief and pride does not concern mutual support.
It challenges the claim that any army can help apart from the Merciful, directly exposing illusory collective support.
It denies a protector or helper apart from God, setting the same boundary of human helplessness.
It immediately confirms the Lord's sentence and the group's shared tasting of punishment.
It explicitly states that the invoked beings cannot help their worshipers or even themselves.
The teaching on disliked fighting does not clarify the focus's failed aid.
The division of water among Thamud does not add to the mutual-help question.
Legal authority for an heir of the slain does not clarify collective aid at judgment.
Invoked beings neither hear nor answer, and disown the association on the Day, supporting the collapse of false reliance.
The misleaders' confession immediately explains how the group led one another into error before punishment.
It denies any protector or helper besides God and therefore reinforces the group’s inability to escape.
The prediction that opponents will not be aided is a distant battle parallel.
The unrestricted giving of the Lord does not clarify the absence of mutual help.
It couples worship without proof with the statement that wrongdoers have no helper, closely fitting the idolaters' judgment.
Salih's completed counsel to Thamud does not develop the mutual-help question.

The promise of divine aid and near victory is a general contrary reference to help.
Satan's promised backing collapses at confrontation, a concrete parallel to an alliance that yields no aid.

The signs of night and day do not clarify support or judgment.

The denial of coolness and drink in Hell does not clarify mutual aid.

The description of untouched companions in Paradise has no relation to the focus.
The prayer names God as protector and asks Him for help, providing the true source of aid against the focus's failure.
It names the scene as the Day of Judgment, supplying the immediate setting for the questions in 37:24-25.
The criminals' refusal to abandon their gods identifies the idolatrous allegiance behind the failed support network.
It states that people take gods besides God in expectation that they will receive help.
It directly overturns that expectation: the gods cannot help them, while their devotees stand as forces for them.
It explicitly says those invoked besides God cannot help their callers or themselves.
It denies that alleged gods can protect even themselves, directly exposing their incapacity as supports.
The judgment question, "Where are those you used to worship?", directly precedes the challenge to their power to help.
The damned confess that they have no intercessors, extending the focus's collapse of expected aid.
The absence of a devoted friend gives a closely related image of abandoned solidarity in the Fire.
The ruined man has no group to help him apart from God and cannot defend himself.
It states that gods besides God were taken in expectation of becoming a source of might.
Those supposed gods will reject their worship and become opponents, reversing the expected alliance.
The taken gods possess neither harm nor benefit, death nor life nor resurrection, explaining why they cannot support anyone.
God gathers the worshipers and their objects of worship and asks whether those objects misled the servants.
The worshiped beings deny the devotees' claim, and the devotees cannot avert punishment or secure help.
The command to call the alleged associates exposes their failure to answer on the Day.
It says that on the Day of Resurrection the associates will be disowned and cursed by one another.

Those invoked besides God possess no share or power, a theological basis for their inability to aid.
The Day's questioning of angels about worship develops the exposure of misplaced devotional alliances.
The rhetorical test of whether invoked beings can remove harm challenges their supposed power to help.
Those invoked besides God do not possess intercession, limiting the aid expected from false objects of worship.
The alleged helpers and near gods fail their worshipers completely and disappear from them.
God gathers the idolaters with their associates and separates them, exposing the broken association at judgment.
Every soul then learns what it sent ahead, and its fabricated associates vanish.
When idolaters see their associates on the Day, they submit their claims and are met with rejection.
The wrongdoers offer submission on that Day and their fabrications disappear, completing the collapse of reliance.
Those invoked besides God cannot remove or redirect harm, directly denying their practical power to help.
Calling on what can neither harm nor benefit depicts reliance on a powerless support.
It calls such a supposed protector and companion an evil reliance, sharpening the focus's failed alliance.
Those invoked besides God cannot answer their callers and remain unaware of their invocation.
On the Day, neither protector nor intercession can ransom the self from judgment.
The claimed protectors besides God cannot benefit or harm even themselves.
Satan disowns authority over his followers, a parallel collapse of a relied-on alliance under judgment.
The gods invoked besides God did not help their worshipers when the Lord's command came.
Those invoked besides God create nothing and are themselves created, undercutting any expectation of help.
The beings invoked seek access to their Lord and cannot remove harm, showing their dependence rather than power to aid.
When the alleged partners are called, they do not answer, and a destructive barrier is set between the parties.
The rebuke asks whether they worship what neither benefits nor harms them, a direct challenge to false reliance.
Calling another god without proof is linked to unavoidable reckoning before the Lord.
People worship besides God what neither benefits nor harms them, directly exposing futile reliance.
The worship of idols is exposed as fabrication while provision comes only from God.
The claimed worship of associates for nearness to God identifies the rationale of the failed intermediary network.
The question about taking intercessors besides God directly challenges reliance on them.
All intercession belongs to God, restricting the help falsely expected from others.
On the Day, invoked beings become enemies of their worshipers and reject their worship.
